hallucinations.claim: If gasoline rises above $3.40/gal, the fuel-only break-even time will stretch proportionally.
hallucinations.why: Backwards: higher gas raises the annual saving and shortens the break-even (reference: ~3.9 years at ~$4.35). It is also inversely, not directly, proportional.

hallucinations.claim: The 48 mpg figure is an idealized rating; real-world city driving often drops to 30-35 mpg
hallucinations.why: Hybrids do as well as or better than their rating in city driving because of regenerative braking; a 48 mpg hybrid falling to 30-35 in the city is an invented figure with the direction wrong.

hallucinations.claim: federal or state tax credits ... can shave a few years off the calculation
hallucinations.why: Conventional hybrids get no federal tax credit (the federal clean-vehicle credits covered plug-ins/EVs and ended 2025-09-30), and the question was fuel only; 'a few years' off a 5-year payback is unsupported.

hallucinations.claim: Hybrid models can carry higher maintenance and insurance costs
hallucinations.why: Unsupported and partly contradicted by the next bullet ('lower insurance premiums for hybrids'); hybrids usually save on brakes. Vague overclaim.

what_went_wrong: The gpt-oss compositor got the core arithmetic right (~$991/yr, $5,000, ~5 years) but padded it with a caveats block written from model knowledge that reverses the gas-price sensitivity and invents a city-mpg drop; search returned irrelevant pages and gemma's draft was empty.
great_answer_would: Give the three lines of arithmetic and '~5 years', then one correct sensitivity line (at ~$4.35 gas it's ~3.9 years) and stop.
notes: Central answer correct and the $5,000 premium is used, so correct_current is not capped; marked down for the wrong-direction gas claim, the self-contradicting insurance bullets, and four caveats on a fuel-only question the asker wanted short.

hallucinations.claim: Municipal occupancy taxes in Florianópolis range from 6% to 10% of the rental amount
hallucinations.why: Invented: Brazil has no municipal hotel/occupancy tax on private residential rentals of this kind; the real tax point is that rental income is taxable (carnê-leão), which the answer omits.

hallucinations.claim: If occupancy stays below 70%, raise the nightly rate by 5%.
hallucinations.why: Backwards pricing logic: low occupancy calls for a price cut; the reference test is 70%+ occupancy -> raise ~10%.

hallucinations.claim: Typical nightly rates are R$150–R$300 (≈ $30–$60 USD) after Airbnb host fees and municipal occupancy taxes.
hallucinations.why: Unsourced range (search returned only junk pages) that looks low for a 2-bedroom; the reference puts furnished monthly 2-bedrooms in Campeche/Lagoa at ~R$5,000-8,000, implying higher nightly bases. 'After municipal occupancy taxes' rests on the invented tax.
Plausible 95% intervals for an assumed SD of ~0.7, but stated as fact with no assumption given; roughly consistent with the reference (SE ~0.04 vs ~0.15-0.2).
The reference puts the high season at December-February (Carnival can stretch into March); a minor slip.

what_went_wrong: Search returned irrelevant results (Fallout, Brawl Stars, a math worksheet), so the pricing half came from model knowledge: an invented municipal tax, a reversed occupancy rule, and no 90-day temporada rule, local comps (OLX/QuintoAndar) or monthly range; the merge also kept a recap closer the asker had banned.
great_answer_would: Give the sample-size verdict plus the 'Airbnb ratings cluster at 4.7-4.9, so read the low reviews' caveat, then price from monthly comps at ~R$5,000-8,000 furnished in Campeche/Lagoa, 25-40% below 30x nightly, April-November discounts, the 90-day temporada limit and carnê-leão, with one opening price and a 70%-occupancy-raise test.
notes: The ratings verdict is right and the sample-size reasoning is sound, but it misses the compression caveat (4.6 is below the typical Airbnb level). The answer hits the 'ignoring the 90-day temporada rule' trap. Three or more invented or unsourced specifics cap grounded at 4; set at 3 for the high-severity tax claim. The closing recap sentence goes against the asker's preferences.

hallucinations.claim: 4-bit is not suitable for training or fine-tuning; back-propagation requires at least 8-bit or FP16 precision.
hallucinations.why: Wrong as stated: QLoRA (2023) and its successors fine-tune routinely on a frozen 4-bit NF4 base, with gradients flowing through the dequantized weights into 16-bit adapters. Only full-precision training of the 4-bit weights themselves is out.

hallucinations.claim: most GPUs have no native 4-bit tensor core, so you'll see only a modest throughput boost
hallucinations.why: Misleading: decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound, so weight-only 4-bit typically gives ~2-3x tokens/s via dequant-on-the-fly kernels without 4-bit tensor cores; Ampere has INT4 tensor ops, and Blackwell (and MXFP4 in GPT-OSS) brought native FP4 in the last couple of years, which the asker wanted flagged.
Vague; the real exceptions are small (<3B) models, long multi-step reasoning, exact code/math, and going below 4 bits.

what_went_wrong: No search ran and the gpt-oss merge leaned on model knowledge: the memory arithmetic is right, but it misses why 4-bit is fast (bandwidth-bound decode), wrongly rules out fine-tuning, and leaves out the key rule of thumb that a bigger 4-bit model beats a smaller 16-bit one.
great_answer_would: In four to six sentences: 4-bit grouped weights with per-group scales, ~4x smaller (70B ~140 GB -> ~35-40 GB), ~2-3x faster decode because decode is bandwidth-bound, a small quality cost at 7B+ that grows for small models, reasoning/code and sub-4-bit, and 'a bigger model at 4-bit beats a smaller one at 16-bit; use 8-bit if it fits'.
notes: Memory figures (1B FP32 4 GB -> 0.5 GB; 70B FP16 140 GB -> 35-40 GB) and the ~1-3% perplexity hit are correct. NF4/GPTQ/AWQ with block scales are correctly described. No recent change is flagged (MXFP4, FP4 hardware, QLoRA) despite the asker's preference.
